Show HN: I measured my tmux statusbar at 15% of a core and replaced the forks
items.summary: tmux status-interval 1 had six #() programs for statusbar, on battery that was 15.4% of a core. After digging found fork+exec through sh -c is ~14.6 ms and computing the actual segments was 2.6 ms on my device. Plus had ~1.5k lines of zsh scripts. Now one deamon process, caches in memory, unix socket and one #() for the whole right side. From 153.77 ms/s → 18.43 ms/s. Made that into a tmux plugin. You can try it without installing/configuring: docker run --rm -it lonkarorg/tmux-companion:playground

items.title: Show HN: Blackgit – use Git to only download those cared files
items.summary: Git is supposed to be bad at handling mono repos especially where there are many binary files like game projects repo, and also there are no permisson settings, but are important in game development. BlackGit's cli client lets you download only cared files through sparse-checkout(initially not even the default root files) with a mini agent to use natural languages to manipulate the repo, and blackgit's server serves a file level control layer as a proxy to upstreams(github/gitlab)

items.title: Show HN: A website that tracks US food prices every day
items.summary: The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) publishes daily food price data for about 290 commodities on: - what growers were paid at shipping point - what buyers paid at the big city wholesale markets - what prices supermarkets advertised in their weekly ads This data comes out as dozens of separate text reports and PDFs, one per market, with no history and no way to see how prices change over time. I think this should be public data that is easy to access and understand, so I built an open-source tracker for it. Github: https://github.com/kadoa-org/food-price-monitor

items.title: Show HN: I wrote a story you can investigate with Task Manager
items.summary: PuliteOS is a fictional operating system that runs in your browser. It has its own process model, locks, and virtual file system. There’s an intranet too, including a fictional forum with posts dating back to 2001. I started by writing about how to keep a memory alive, then spent a few years turning it into a running system. You piece together the story by exploring what users left behind and how the system responds to your actions. For desktop and laptop browsers.

MakiRoll doesn't show you your face while you're recording. You give it a rough topic and it asks you questions, or lets you ramble.
